summary: A prologue in two parts: first a note about how this Greek text of Esther reached Egypt, then Mordecai's dream — tumults and thunders, two great dragons ready to fight, the nations stirred against 'the nation of the just,' and then a little fountain growing into a river, the sun rising, and the humble devouring the glorious. Mordecai wakes and keeps the dream in mind, 'desirous to know what the dream should signify.'
whyItMatters: The Hebrew Esther never mentions God and reads like pure coincidence; this Greek opening reframes the whole book as prophecy — the dream is the plot in code, and by chapter 21 the text will tell you exactly what it meant. The additions turn a court story into a theology of providence.

context.author: Unknown Jewish author writing in Greek; the prologue names Dositheus and Ptolemy as its Egyptian carriers
context.date: The translation note points to the late 2nd century BC (Ptolemy and Cleopatra)
context.setting: Susa (Susan), the Persian capital, in the days of Artaxerxes

keyVerses.text: And behold two great dragons came forth ready to fight one against another. And at their cry all nations were stirred up to fight against the nation of the just.
keyVerses.why: The dream's central image — by chapter 21 the text decodes it: the dragons are Mardochai and Aman.

keyVerses.text: And they cried to God: and as they were crying, a little fountain grew into a very great river, and abounded into many waters.
keyVerses.why: Deliverance begins as something small — a fountain — while the just are still crying out. The image carries the book's theology of providence.

keyVerses.text: And when Mardochai had seen this, and arose out of his bed, he was thinking what God would do: and he kept it fixed in his mind, desirous to know what the dream should signify.
keyVerses.why: Note the word 'God' — the Hebrew book never uses it. The additions exist, in large part, to say this word.

themes: God named where he was hidden

questions.question: Why doesn't my Bible have this chapter?
questions.answer: The Hebrew book of Esther has ten chapters and never mentions God. Greek-speaking Jews added six chapters (prologue, prayers, and letters) in their Septuagint translation. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles keep them; Protestant Bibles follow the shorter Hebrew text. In this 16-chapter arrangement they are chapters 11-16.

questions.question: What do the two dragons mean?
questions.answer: The text itself interprets later: chapter 21 says the dream showed 'two great dragons' — 'thy servant Mardochai' and 'this wicked Aman.' The nations stirred up are the empire's peoples under the decree; the little fountain is Israel's cry for help becoming a river of deliverance.

questions.question: Who are Ptolemy and Cleopatra in verse 1?
questions.answer: The Ptolemies ruled Egypt after Alexander's empire split; the pairing points to the late second century BC. The note is the Greek translator's way of certifying his source — a letter of Purim brought from Jerusalem, interpreted by Lysimachus. It is a claim: this text comes from the holy city, not from Alexandria's imagination.

questions.question: Why frame the story as a dream at all?
questions.answer: Dreams in Scripture announce what God is about to do — Joseph, Daniel, the Magi. By opening with one, the Greek Esther tells you before the plot starts: the coincidences ahead are not coincidences. The Hebrew book makes you feel God's hiddenness; the Greek book makes you see his hand.

questions.question: Who is Jechonias in verse 4?
questions.answer: Jehoiachin, the king of Judah exiled to Babylon in 597 BC. Mordecai's family went into that early deportation — meaning Mordecai belongs to a family nearly 120 years in exile, a courtier whose loyalty to Jerusalem survived four generations of Babylon and Persia.
